newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Nordic EU trio debate ERM links. [CORRECTED 14:30 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Nordic EU trio debate ERM links. [CORRECTED 14:30 GMT]

text.p: The European Union's three Nordic members, with different currency policy pasts and varying degrees of economic strength, are all debating possible closer links with the bloc's exchange rate mechanism (ERM).
Like other European countries, Denmark, Sweden and Finland are considering their options as the 15-nation EU prepares for the final stage of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"The link is that monetary union is approaching," said economist Wike Groenenberg at investment bank Salomon Brothers (corrects name of bank from Morgan Stanley).

Denmark, already in the present ERM which limits fluctuations between participating currencies, has decided not to join monetary union and will instead seek a close relationship with the planned single currency.

Copenhagen therefore takes keen interest in a new currency mechanism, dubbed "ERM2", which will be set up to link countries outside EMU with the euro currency, saying the crown should trade within narrow bands.

Finland, determined to be among the first to join monetary union, may decide soon to link the markka to the current ERM as it seeks to fulfil all the requirements laid down in the EU's Maastricht treaty for taking part in the single currency.

In Sweden, Central Bank governor Urban Backstrom last week injected new life into fading market speculation about possible ERM membership, listing potential benefits of such a move, even though he reiterated that entry was not topical now.

"I believe that the time is ready to start discussing this issue because Sweden has become an increasingly stable country," Backstrom told Reuters during the weekend meeting of EU finance ministers and central bank heads in Dublin.
Reacting to his remarks, Morgan Stanley's Groenenberg said: "His comments were rather strongly worded in favour of Sweden joining the ERM."
Finland and Sweden, whose currencies are floating, only joined the EU last year while Denmark is a member since 1973.
There was consensus at the Dublin meeting, which laid the foundations for critical areas of monetary union, on the outline for the new ERM.
Ministers agreed that it should be voluntary and include relatively wide trading bands for currencies outside EMU.
However, Denmark -- one of only a few EU countries which currently qualify for monetary union -- could enter with narrower fluctuation bands than the standard ones.
Economy Minister Marianne Jelved, who had expressed concern ahead of the meeting, said she was satisfied with the talks.
"It seems like we can get a bilateral agreement between the ECB (the future European Central Bank) and the Danish National Bank and government," she told Reuters.

Jelved had earlier said she liked the way the ERM worked before the currency turmoil of 1993 when it had fluctuation margins of 2.25 percent up or down for most participating currencies. The bands are now 15 percent.
Finland is widely expected to join the present ERM soon.
There was even market speculation that this would happen during the weekend meeting in Dublin but Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto told Reuters the issue had not been discussed.
Any decision to join the ERM seems to be further away in neighbouring Sweden even if Backstrom said he personally believed such a move would be desirable later.

ERM membership could underscore Sweden's increased economic stability and also further demonstrate its determination to continue with a policy aimed at low inflation and sound public finances also if it opted to stay outside EMU, he said.

But he said it was important to have support in the Swedish society for any decision to join the ERM, which currently groups 10 of the EU's 15 member countries. "We will see how that discussion is developing," he said.
Backstrom noted that there were critical voices in the current Swedish debate and he suggested that Sweden could not join ERM if there was strong opposition.
